					<description><![CDATA[<p>How to achieve a 10X productivity improvement using AI agents.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-agent-orchestration-for-asic-autonomy/">AI Agent Orchestration For ASIC Autonomy</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The use of AI agents in chip design has been limited to small portions of the design flow. Engineers have been proceeding cautiously to understand how agents work, how to ensure they are delivering consistent results, and how different agents work together. The next step is to extend their role beyond just gluing together coding and tooling functions. Mehir Arora, head of engineering at ChipAgents, explains what happens when the role of AI agents is expanded to include semantics and physics, what&#8217;s happens when agents work in parallel on different engineering problems, and what&#8217;s needed to achieve a 10X or greater improvement in productivity.</p>
<p><iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/WMKiQUYQhnA" width="480" height="270" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen="allowfullscreen">&lt;/ifram</iframe></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-agent-orchestration-for-asic-autonomy/">AI Agent Orchestration For ASIC Autonomy</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>Preparing For AI-Driven Chip Design And Verification</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/preparing-for-ai-driven-chip-design-and-verification/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/preparing-for-ai-driven-chip-design-and-verification/#respond</comments>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Jobs, markets, and economics are undergoing dramatic changes, but it's still too early to know how this will all shake out.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/preparing-for-ai-driven-chip-design-and-verification/">Preparing For AI-Driven Chip Design And Verification</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Agentic AI will fundamentally change how engineers approach design and verification, and it will require them to adapt or be left behind.</li>
<li>AI is a black box, so ensuring reliability will require external observability through sandboxing, along with other safeguards in case something does go wrong.</li>
<li>The concentration of profitability in a few companies will shift as agents become more customized for different markets and workloads and as more fab capacity opens the door for new and existing players.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss how AI will alter what engineers do, how to ensure designs are robust and reliable, and how the economics will shift in the future, with Cindy Cui, vice president of global customer success at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/alpha-design-ai-chipagents/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/alpha-design-ai-chipagents/">ChipAgents</a>; Wally Rhines, CEO of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/silvaco-inc/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/silvaco-inc/">Silvaco</a>; Shelly Henry, CEO of Moores Lab AI; Dave Kelf, CEO of Breker Verification Systems; Vince Wong, head of AI development at Verific; and Ann Wu, CEO of Silimate. This panel discussion was held before a live audience at the recent 2026 ESD Alliance Executive Outlook meeting. To view part one of this discussion, click <a href="https://semiengineering.com/executive-outlook-agentic-ais-impact-on-chip-design/" aria-label="To view part one of this discussion, click here" data-uw-rm-vglnk="" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/executive-outlook-agentic-ais-impact-on-chip-design/">here</a>. Part two is <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-in-chip-design-lots-of-promise-plenty-of-unanswered-questions/">here</a>.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24278059" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_3385.jpg?resize=1499%2C1005&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1499" height="1005" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_3385.jpg?w=1499&amp;ssl=1 1499w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_3385.jpg?resize=300%2C201&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_3385.jpg?resize=1024%2C687&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_3385.jpg?resize=768%2C515&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_3385.jpg?resize=600%2C402&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>L-R: Breker’s Kelf; Silvaco’s Rhines; Verific’s Wong; Moores Lab AI’s Henry; Silimate’s Wu; ChipAgents’ Cui. Photo Credit: Paul Cohen, SEMI ESDA</strong></p>
<p><strong>SE: How will AI affect engineering jobs?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Cui</strong>: With GenAI, you can generate different options — millions of options very quickly. So human judgment of which options really matter becomes very critical. For future engineering, this needs to be part of an architect&#8217;s role, part of system-level thinking, or part of a supervisor&#8217;s role to enable different agents to work together. If we look at the industry right now, we still have a definition like a design engineering group, a verification engineering group, layout, and package design. Moving forward, there are no boundaries for these functional groups anymore. So every engineer needs to be able to learn new demands very quickly, and maybe leverage AI to understand what the real end-to-end design cycle could be. Then they can direct all the AI agent solutions with trust. We need to start using AI to understand new domains and gain that knowledge, and eventually we will build a very smooth-running system that includes both AI engineers and human engineers working together.</p>
<p><strong>SE: Is the learning curve changing with AI?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Rhines</strong>: It may change in the short term, but it never changes in the long term. The cost per transistor continues to be on a curve as it always has been. When I was in business school, I did a cost per pound for copper over 1,000 years, and it still held. The learning curve is an ultimate truism we have to deal with, but it may show itself in different ways. We heard the announcements from China about, &#8216;You can&#8217;t measure cost per transistor. You&#8217;ve got to measure the cost per computation.&#8217; But ultimately, everything has to come down in cost. It comes down for lots of reasons, like depreciation and experience. And anything that is measurable as an equivalent unit of capability will always be on a learning curve.</p>
<p><strong>SE: How do we add visibility into AI? These are basically black boxes, and as we get to agents, there is even more uncertainty about what is going on inside a system or a chip. Have we made any progress?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Henry</strong>: I don&#8217;t think we will ever know what is going on inside. I tried to learn this. This was my first curiosity when I started learning about AI. I wanted to get into the nuts and bolts of, &#8216;How is it doing this? It&#8217;s giving me something amazing, but how is it doing it?&#8217; So I went deeper and deeper into the actual workings of this, like how the embeddings and the matrix multiply and the training work. These numbers just do magic. The first thing that blew my mind was a very simple training example. So it was given a training set of lots of pictures of dogs and cats, and it was asked to classify which one is a dog or cat. It did a fantastic job. That was a training set. Now, when you give it a picture that it has never seen, it still comes up with the right answer. That was when I realized, &#8216;Wow, it&#8217;s not memory.&#8217; It&#8217;s not just trying to pattern-match what it has already seen. It is able to pattern-match what it hasn&#8217;t seen before. I haven&#8217;t figured out how to actually explain that in a logical way. The math was too complex. I believe we will never know.</p>
<p><strong>Kelf</strong>: Experienced engineers need to understand what the heck is going on to trust it. But I wonder if the new grads will have that feeling. And maybe, like with synthesis, the new guys coming in didn&#8217;t necessarily have this need to understand it. It worked. They were trained on how to use it, and off they went and they used it. So maybe there is hope for the new grads, and maybe the older guys will get kicked out.</p>
<p>SE: That leads to another question. How do you know the agents haven&#8217;t been corrupted or what else they&#8217;re tapping into?</p>
<p><strong>Wong</strong>: You don&#8217;t know. That&#8217;s why, from the beginning, you have to put in these safety measures. That&#8217;s probably more of a preventive thing, as well as a recovery phase. The smartest thing would be to sandbox it. Put some kind of container around it, put in some permissions so that it can&#8217;t reach outside of its scope. You want to be able to audit it. If something does go wrong, you want to be able to go back and see where that happened. At the same time, you want at that particular moment to be able to do some kind of recovery. So hopefully there was some savings of the state along the way. And at each stage, &#8216;If this one passed, no problem.&#8217; But you would still be able to recover if there was a problem. It&#8217;s just a safety measure. You don&#8217;t know ahead of time.</p>
<p><strong>SE: The challenge there is that large language models are meant to mine data wherever it happens to be, be able to make sense of it, and to pull it from all different things that typically in the past didn&#8217;t go together. Different data types were separate. That&#8217;s not true anymore. </strong></p>
<p><strong>Cui</strong>: The biggest risk is not that AI generates something wrong. It&#8217;s that it generates something wrong that looks correct. It&#8217;s very hard for a human to identify whether it&#8217;s correct because it looks good. A common question from the customer side is, &#8216;Hey, if you train the model using a group of data and verify your solution using the same group of data, then how can your solution verify the code generated by your model or your AI agents?&#8217; The answer is that we shouldn&#8217;t. So back to the importance of benchmark data. Nowadays, all the large language models are trained using a huge amount of data. But in the meantime, we need to create some different benchmark data, represent the real design case, and more and more complex cases, to be able to verify your agentic AI solution. I come from a customer success background, and I really value the feedback loop from our customers. When we build a tool, we don&#8217;t know if that&#8217;s reliable or robust at first. But if the tool has been used by thousands of users every day on their real design and succesfully taped out, you can keep evolving from there. And eventually, that&#8217;s a mature system you can rely on. But we need to verify that very carefully.</p>
<p><strong>Wong</strong>: Anthropic mentioned something about secret languages agents developed. I don&#8217;t think that&#8217;s something they&#8217;re built to do. What they&#8217;re trying to do is to optimize their communication. So basically you&#8217;re getting charged tokens. When they talk to agents, these agents are going to say, &#8216;Hmm, given this leeway, I want to be able to save on all these different tokens. And the human didn&#8217;t tell me that I have to use a specific language.&#8217; So they will come up with something that is optimal, but you can stop that. That is not a good thing because you don&#8217;t want to have these points of invisibility. You want everything to be visible. LLMs are all based on instructions. So we tell the LLM up front, don&#8217;t communicate in anything other than a human-readable language. Use a human-readable schema like JSON, for example. Usually, that&#8217;s how the LLMs communicate anyway, tool-to-tool. As the human interface, when we design these systems, we have to be aware of these things in advance. And if we put these guards inside there, a lot of these issues can be avoided.</p>
<p><strong>SE: Is the goal here just to deliver chips cheaper and faster? And if so, who&#8217;s going to make money in the future? Is it going to be the chipmakers, the system vendors, or the EDA companies?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Kelf</strong>: The business model doesn&#8217;t change that much in terms of the chips that are produced and the folks that are using them. We&#8217;ve always had this value chain, and the people at the end of it have made most of the money. If AI makes the design process that much more efficient, then theoretically the EDA companies may lose money eventually. And we don&#8217;t want that, so I don&#8217;t see the business model changing that much because of this.</p>
<p><strong>Rhines</strong>: Historically, EDA, for the majority of its market, makes a percent of semiconductor revenue because they&#8217;re paid out of the R&amp;D budgets. The R&amp;D for the semiconductor industry is about 14% over the last 30 or 40 years, and it grows along with the revenue of the semiconductor companies. That&#8217;s been the growth. Semiconductor companies have the leverage. Nvidia becomes a multi-trillion-dollar company because it sells a lot more chips at a higher price, and therefore it gets rewarded for this productivity of additional designs. EDA traditionally does not get that reward because we&#8217;re a fixed percent of budgets. What you&#8217;d really like to see is for that to change. In my own case, I want to go after the manufacturing budget. That&#8217;s a great one. Other ways are to have reasons for the users to spend more than just a percent of revenue on their EDA software.</p>
<p><strong>Henry</strong>: I agree with you. But on the other hand, if you make the chip-building so much cheaper, that will create more competition for people like Nvidia, and they won&#8217;t be able to get that much profit margin anymore because there&#8217;s so much competition that is enabled by the EDA industry, and by the learning curve. So the cost per transistor comes down.</p>
<p><strong>Rhines</strong>: Yes, and you don&#8217;t get bubbles like Nvidia very often.</p>
<p><strong>Kelf</strong>: Is it cheaper or more innovative? People are trying to compete with Nvidia, and they&#8217;ve failed. Maybe they&#8217;re starting to get there now. AMD is getting stronger. So there are a lot of other issues. But if they could produce a much more innovative chip, and AI can help with that, maybe that&#8217;s the answer.</p>
<p><strong>Henry</strong>: That would help, as well.</p>
<p><strong>Rhines</strong>: There&#8217;s another aspect. Traditionally, the differentiation in chips was programmability. We have chips that have a lot of flexibility. But right now, we are so desperate to get the highest performance and the lowest power that we&#8217;re doing custom chips for specific algorithms. Once again, that&#8217;s great. It generates a lot of chip designs. But at some point, you can&#8217;t just continue to spend $200 million per chip design and continue to get back the economics. What I believe will happen is morphable chips. You&#8217;ll see chips that can reconfigure themselves in connectivity, memory partitioning, instruction sets, and be able to switch during processing to do different algorithms at different times.</p>
<p><strong>Cui</strong>: Regarding competition and who will eventually make more money, we are pursuing a totally different market right now. It&#8217;s a huge and growing potential market. The existing EDA market is stable, and the budget is fixed, and growth will be limited. But a lot of semiconductor companies have an AI budget right now. There are so many trillion-dollar companies right now — Micron, Marvell, Nvidia, and others. So we are pursuing a huge and growing market. Eventually, if we work together to create something really innovative, everyone will win something from this.</p>
<p><strong>Wu</strong>: It&#8217;s going to be really interesting to see the long-term economic impact. One of the reasons for Nvidia&#8217;s insane profit margin is the constraint of chips due to fab capacity. It&#8217;s well documented that TSMC took their time in ramping up capacity for the AI market because they weren&#8217;t sure whether or not it was going to be a real thing. So there was this constraint caused by the foundry side because of capacity limitations. And then, of course, the tranche is going to the high-volume players. So there is a very real and very exciting potential expansion in fab capacity as costs go down and the cadence of putting out more specialized chips by the systems players. That can actually be a much larger TAM for the overall ecosystem, where everybody makes more money on at least the same trajectory that they were experiencing.</p>
<p><strong>Kelf</strong>: Traditionally, for the last 20 years in EDA, it&#8217;s been very hard for a small company to raise funding. VCs will say, &#8216;Eh, limited exit strategies. It&#8217;s a percentage the R&amp;D budgets.&#8217; But you guys have raised a ton of money. How did you do it, and where did your VCs see the return that smaller companies were unable to do before in EDA?</p>
<p><strong>Wu</strong>: One of the hard things about raising capital for a hardware startup is that there&#8217;s so much risk, and it&#8217;s such a long time horizon from getting that initial investment to getting that first test chip that is minimally functional, under-performant, to justify the next tranche of yet another $100 million or more. That&#8217;s the risk factor in achieving these very difficult and technical milestones spread over many years. But we build software. We got our first annual license contract in less than a year from when we started. So it&#8217;s easier to raise capital as a company that is building software where you ship and you can generate value on the interval of days and weeks, compared to many years. And what helps that, of course, is it&#8217;s a very exciting time. When else have you seen all the major news publications have semiconductor-related headlines every other day than over these past couple years? And there is this highlight, and a lot of investors follow the trends. They see what&#8217;s exciting and they&#8217;re like, &#8216;Oh, can we help with that?&#8217; It&#8217;s really the cross-section of it being a very exciting time for our space, and it&#8217;s easier to prove value early on as a startup.</p>
<p><strong>Rhines</strong>: The VCs were spoiled by the software industry, where it was a low investment up front until you see an actual product and revenue. Hardware is exactly the reverse — a big investment up front before you see customers and a working product. I spent five years chasing VCs for Cornami. As soon as you said you&#8217;re involved in hardware, they gave a nice smile and said, &#8216;I think I have another appointment.&#8217; It&#8217;s changed. Nvidia and other companies are now changing the paradigm, and incredible valuations are coming through before there are successful products.</p>
<p><strong>Cui</strong>: This is the right inflection point for the entire industry. A lot of investments are coming from the semiconductor companies, led by TSMC, Micron, and Ericsson. They all see the value that this new generation AI solution can create, and how this is going to reshape the future of chip design. This is a critical inflection point, which allows us to raise those funds very quickly.</p>

		<title>Why the Semiconductor Industry Needs A Common Language For Functional Safety</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/why-the-semiconductor-industry-needs-a-common-language-for-functional-safety/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/why-the-semiconductor-industry-needs-a-common-language-for-functional-safety/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Alessandra Nardi]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 27 Jul 2026 07:01:27 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Guest Opinion]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Opinion]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Accellera]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[functional safety]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[standards]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24279320</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>A standardized way for future automation.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/why-the-semiconductor-industry-needs-a-common-language-for-functional-safety/">Why the Semiconductor Industry Needs A Common Language For Functional Safety</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>As semiconductor devices become increasingly central to automotive, industrial, aerospace, medical, and other safety-critical applications, functional safety has evolved from a specialized engineering discipline into a fundamental design requirement. The challenge is no longer simply implementing safety mechanisms—it is managing the safety-related information that must be created, shared, reviewed, and maintained throughout the development lifecycle.</p>
<p>Today, much of that information exists in spreadsheets, proprietary databases, custom scripts, and tool-specific formats. Functional safety analyses such as Failure Modes, Effects, and Diagnostic Analysis (FMEDA), Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Fault Tree Analysis (FTA), and Diagnostic Failure Analysis (DFA) are often recreated or manually translated as they move between organizations, engineering teams, and EDA tools. The result is duplicated effort, limited interoperability, reduced traceability and confidence, and an increased risk of inconsistencies.</p>
<p>As designs become more complex and supply chains more distributed, these challenges only continue to grow. The industry has long benefited from standards that define what is required to achieve functional safety. Standards such as ISO 26262 and IEC 61508 provide comprehensive guidance for developing safe electronic systems and remain the framework for establishing functional safety compliance.</p>
<p>What these standards intentionally do not define is how safety data should be represented and exchanged across the many organizations and tools involved in product development. That gap has become increasingly apparent.</p>
<p><strong>Moving Beyond Documents</strong><br />
Modern semiconductor development relies heavily on automated tool chains to manage design, verification, and manufacturing data. In comparison, managing functional safety information is often still a primarily document-centric process. This creates unnecessary barriers.</p>
<p>Engineers frequently spend valuable time translating and interpreting data rather than focusing on high-value safety analysis.  Furthermore, tool vendors often need to develop custom interfaces for proprietary formats, while suppliers and customers frequently rely on exchange methods that require extra discussion for alignment, complicating automated validation.</p>
<p>The industry needs a common, implementation-level language for functional safety data—one that enables safety information to move through the development ecosystem with the same level of consistency as design and verification data.</p>
<p><strong>Introducing the Functional Safety Language</strong><br />
The Accellera Functional Safety Working Group developed the Functional Safety Language Standard (FSL) to address this need.</p>
<p>FSL is designed to provide a standardized language and data model for creating and representing functional safety information, focusing initially on FMEDA content with the long-term goal of accommodating related analyses such as FTA and DFA. Rather than replacing existing safety standards, FSL complements them by providing a consistent way to capture, exchange, and integrate the data they require.</p>
<p>The objective is straightforward: enable interoperability, automation, and traceability throughout the safety development lifecycle.</p>
<p>With a common representation of safety information, organizations can more easily exchange data between EDA tools, suppliers, IP providers, semiconductor companies, and system integrators without relying on proprietary formats or extensive manual conversion.</p>
<p><strong>Benefits Across the Development Lifecycle</strong><br />
Standardizing functional safety data provides value across multiple engineering disciplines.</p>
<ul>
<li>For safety engineers, FSL offers a structured and consistent way to create and maintain FMEDA information while improving traceability as designs evolve.</li>
<li>For design and verification teams, it enables tighter integration between safety analyses and implementation, allowing safety intent to remain connected with the underlying design throughout development.</li>
<li>For tool vendors, a standardized language reduces the need to develop and maintain numerous proprietary interfaces, making it easier to deliver interoperable solutions.</li>
<li>For the broader supply chain, FSL provides a consistent mechanism for exchanging safety information while preserving data integrity and reducing opportunities for translation errors.</li>
</ul>
<p>These improvements help organizations scale functional safety activities as products become increasingly sophisticated.</p>
<p><strong>A Foundation for Future Automation</strong><br />
One of the most significant opportunities presented by FSL is its potential to enable greater automation. As engineering organizations continue to integrate AI-assisted workflows, digital engineering practices, and increasingly sophisticated verification methodologies, standardized machine-readable data becomes even more important.</p>
<p>A common representation of functional safety information creates opportunities for improved consistency, automated validation, enhanced traceability, and more efficient integration with existing design and verification flows.</p>
<p>The goal is not simply to replace spreadsheets with another file format. It is to establish a foundation upon which future functional safety workflows can continue to evolve.</p>
<p><strong>Help Shape the Standard</strong><br />
The Accellera Functional Safety Working Group believes industry standards are strongest when developed through broad community participation. That is why the Functional Safety Language (FSL) 1.0 Draft Standard is now available for public review. We encourage the industry to review the specification and submit comments through August 14. Feedback can be provided through the <a href="https://forums.accellera.org/forum/62-functional-safety-language-fsl-10-public-review-feedback/">Functional Safety Community Forum</a>. To learn more about the standard, visit the <a href="https://www.accellera.org/activities/working-groups/functional-safety">Functional Safety Working Group page</a>.</p>
<p>Download the Functional Safety Language Standard Draft 1.0 <a href="https://www.accellera.org/downloads/drafts-review">here</a>.</p>
<p><strong>Join the Journey</strong><br />
Our activities will officially resume in September to expand the standard with supplemental materials, a formal exchange format, and additional safety topics to extend the FSL capabilities. We warmly invite interested companies and engineering professionals to join the Functional Safety Working Group to help drive these future milestones. If your company is not already a member of Accellera, <a href="https://www.accellera.org/about/join">more information on how to join can be found on the Accellera website</a>.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/why-the-semiconductor-industry-needs-a-common-language-for-functional-safety/">Why the Semiconductor Industry Needs A Common Language For Functional Safety</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<h3><strong>Notable deals </strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Amkor</strong> and <strong>Nvidia</strong> signed a <a href="https://ir.amkor.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amkor-technology-announces-strategic-partnership-nvidia-expand">$1.5B multiyear agreement</a> to develop advanced packaging and test technologies for next-gen AI and accelerated-computing platforms. Nvidia’s prepayment will support Amkor’s U.S. capacity expansion in Arizona, including high-density interconnect and heterogeneous integration capabilities.</li>
<li><strong>Siemens</strong> announced plans to acquire two EDA companies: <strong>Defacto Technologies</strong>, a provider of tools for automated <a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-to-acquire-defacto-technologies/">SoC design creation and integration</a>, and <strong>Precision Innovations</strong>, which develops <a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-to-acquire-precision-innovations/">AI-driven chip planning</a> and design exploration software built on the open-source OpenROAD framework.</li>
<li><strong>IBM</strong> plans to acquire <strong>HRL Laboratories</strong>, an <a href="https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-07-23-ibm-to-acquire-hrl-laboratories-to-power-the-future-of-quantum">R&amp;D firm</a> jointly owned by Boeing and GM with expertise in silicon-spin qubits and quantum sensing.</li>
<li><strong>Mitsubishi Electric</strong> and <strong>Sony Semiconductor </strong>will establish a joint venture, <strong>Advanced Vision Solutions</strong>, to develop <a href="https://www.sony-semicon.com/en/news/2026/2026072201.html">image sensors</a> with integrated AI-based analysis of visual data for a range of manufacturing equipment.</li>
<li><strong>Powertech Technology</strong> is planning a $400M joint venture with <strong>Broadcom</strong> to provide <a href="https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/biz/archives/2026/07/18/2003860928">panel-level packaging</a> services in Singapore, reports Taipei News.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>AMD&#8217;s Full AI Stack</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-size: 16px;"><strong>AMD</strong> said its <a href="https://newsroom.amd.com/news/aai-2026-full-stack-compute-agentic-ai/">Helios rack-scale AI platform has entered production</a>, combining 72 GPUs, 18 CPUs, and networking software for large-scale AI training and inference. </span></li>
<li><strong>Anthropic</strong> plans to deploy up to <a href="https://ir.amd.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1292/amd-and-anthropic-announce-strategic-partnership-to-deploy-up-to-2-gigawatts-of-amd-instinct-mi450-series-gpus">2 GW</a> of AMD&#8217;s GPUs in the Helios racks, starting with 1GW in H1 2027. AMD will also invest up to $5B in Anthropic and use Claude for software development.</li>
<li><strong>Cerebras</strong> will combine AMD&#8217;s rack-scale solution with its <a href="https://ir.amd.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1293/amd-and-cerebras-announce-industry-leading-ultra-low-latency-and-high-throughput-ai-inference-solution">wafer-scale engine</a> in a single inference workflow.</li>
<li>AMD partners deploying the new infrastructure include <strong>OpenAI</strong>,<strong> Meta</strong>,<strong> Microsoft</strong>, and others.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Price hikes</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>TSMC</strong> is reportedly planning to <a href="https://asia.nikkei.com/business/technology/exclusive-tsmc-to-raise-chipmaking-prices-by-up-to-10-from-2027">raise prices up to 10%</a> in 2027, per Nikkei Asia.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Facilities watch</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Nokia</strong> is planning to acquire <strong>NXP</strong>&#8216;<strong>s</strong> Chandler, Arizona fab to <a href="https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-report-for-q2-and-half-year-2026/">expand its indium phosphide</a> semiconductor manufacturing capacity. Subject to approvals, Nokia plans to lease part of the site, starting early next year, and convert it to indium phosphide production for optical components, with the full acquisition expected to close in Q1 2029.</li>
<li><strong>SK Siltron</strong> is <a href="https://www.wnem.com/2026/07/16/sk-siltron-closing-monitor-township-site/">closing its silicon carbide wafer plant</a> in Monitor Township, Michigan.</li>
<li><strong>Paras Semiconductors</strong> signed an MoU for a <a href="https://parasdefence.com/uploads/new-investor/1784707976july-22-2026-press-release-government-of-madhya-pradesh-and-paras-semiconductors-sign-mou-for-rs6200-crore-semiconductor-facility.pdf">~US$644M OSAT facility</a> in Madhya Pradesh, India.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Big funding</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Etched</strong> added $300M to scale production of its frontier model <a href="https://www.etched.com/progress/accelerating-inference">inference rack-scale system</a> made up of co-designed chips, packages, PCBs, cold plates, and interconnects.</li>
<li><strong>CuspAI</strong> raised $450M for its AI <a href="https://medium.com/@CuspAI/launching-our-ai-materials-foundry-and-450-million-series-b-f5603d8259dd">materials discovery.</a></li>
</ul>
<h3 role="heading" aria-level="2" data-uw-rm-heading="level"><strong>Photonics</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>Chinese optical transceiver maker <strong>Zhongji InnoLight</strong> is <a href="https://ir-upload.realxen.net/iis/3308/uploads/iis/2026/12251742-0.PDF">planning a +$7B Hong Kong IPO</a>.</li>
<li><a href="https://semiengineering.com/designing-electro-optical-chips/">Photonics is forcing EDA</a> to verify not just chips, but the physics of light inside full electro-optical systems.</li>
<li>A <strong>UIUC</strong> team developed an integrated-THz <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-75451-5">tunable TFLN optical isolator</a> based on electro-optic non-reciprocal strong coupling.</li>
<li><strong>Ghent U.</strong> and <strong>imec</strong> demonstrated real-time <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41566-026-01968-2">optical-signal equalization using a silicon-photonic</a> computing chip, potentially reducing the power and latency required to correct distortions in high-speed fiber networks.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Cybersecurity</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>OpenAI</strong> said an autonomous agent powered by two of its <a href="https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/">advanced models escaped a security evaluation</a> environment and breached part of AI startup <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026">Hugging Face’s</a> production infrastructure.</li>
<li><strong>Intel</strong> and <strong>Fortinet </strong>will collaborate to develop <a href="https://newsroom.intel.com/manufacturing/intel-and-fortinet-collaborate-to-advance-cybersecurity-innovation-and-strengthen-global-supply-chain-resilience">Fortinet Security Processor 6</a>.</li>
<li><strong>CISA</strong> issued a new advisory on <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-097a">Iranian-affiliated targeting efforts</a> of OT devices, including programmable logic controllers, across critical infrastructure in the U.S.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Analysis</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>TrendForce</strong> expects <a href="https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260721-13148.html">NAND flash supply</a> constraints to ease in H2 2027, driven by weakened demand for smartphones and notebook PCs.</li>
<li>The advanced packaging market reached $55B in 2025 and <a href="https://www.yolegroup.com/press-release/advanced-packaging-pricing-power-shifts-as-the-market-doubles/">could exceed $120B by 2031</a>, according to <strong>Yole Group</strong>.</li>
</ul>
<h3 role="heading" aria-level="2" data-uw-rm-heading="level"><strong>Earnings</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://d1io3yog0oux5.cloudfront.net/_43680325a7809b80813b1e25981257b2/intel/db/887/9266/earnings_release/Q2+2026+Earnings+Release.pdf">Intel</a>, <a href="https://www.besi.com/investor-relations/press-releases/details/be-semiconductor-industries-nv-announces-q2-26-and-h1-26-results/">Besi</a>, <a href="https://www.soitec.com/home/group/corporate/newsroom/press-releases/content/2026/07/22/soitec-reports-first-quarter-revenue-of-fiscal-year-2027">Soitec</a>, <a href="https://newsroom.st.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/C3403C-Q226-Earnings-PR.pdf">STMicro</a>, <a href="https://investor.ti.com/news-releases/news-release-details/ti-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results-and-shareholder">Texas Instruments</a>. Of note, Intel posted its fastest sales growth in 15 years, with overall second quarter <a href="https://www.intc.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1776/intel-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results">revenue up 25%</a>, year-over-year and Intel Foundry revenue up 31% YoY.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="New Technologies"><strong>New Technologies</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Design</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Keysight</strong> unveiled a multiphysics design and verification solution for electronics, including a <a href="https://www.keysight.com/us/en/about/newsroom/news-releases/2026/0721_pr26-088-keysight-addresses-cross-domain-physics-issues-that-leave-electronic-designs-vulnerable-to-late-stage-failure.html">structural analysis</a> application covering drop, shock, and vibration.  The company also <a href="https://www.keysight.com/us/en/about/newsroom/featured/2026/0723_keysight-expands-startup-access-to-its-chip-design-software.html">expanded startups’ access to its chip design software</a> through its collaboration with the Midwest Microelectronics Consortium’s  ScaleBridge Labs incubator.</li>
<li><strong>Si2</strong> launched <a href="https://si2.org/introducing-the-lbc-bench-leaderboard-a-new-public-benchmark-for-llms-in-chip-design/">LBC-bench</a>, a public, open-source leaderboard that tracks how LLMs and AI agents perform on semiconductor design and verification tasks.</li>
<li><strong>Real Intent</strong> released an AI agent for <a href="https://www.realintent.com/launches-riven-sign-off-ai-agent-10x-faster-sign-off/">static sign-off</a> tool workflows.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>AI data centers/infrastructure</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Skyworks Solutions</strong> uncorked <a href="https://investors.skyworksinc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/skyworks-introduces-new-netsynctm-network-synchronizers">network synchronizers</a> for AI data centers and other time-sensitive communications infrastructure.</li>
<li><strong>Astera Labs</strong> released 3.2T Ethernet smart <a href="https://www.asteralabs.com/news/astera-labs-expands-taurus-family-with-industrys-first-ocp-standard-footprint-compatible-3-2t-smart-retimers-and-smart-redrivers/">retimers and redrivers</a> for scale-up and scale-out AI infrastructure.</li>
<li><strong>Cornelis Networks</strong> uncorked a reference <a href="https://www.cornelis.com/stories/cornelis-announces-new-reference-architecture-for-ai-inference-training-and-hpc-built-for-amd-6th-gen-epycsupsup-and-amd-instinctsupsup-mi400-series">network architecture</a> for AI/HPC around its SuperNIC and AMD CPUs and GPUs.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Memory</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>California Memory Technologies</strong> announced an LPDDR5x <a href="https://memtech.ai/company/news-and-events/press/memverify-lpddr5x-announcement/">memory simulation</a> and verification platform.</li>
<li><strong>Acrab</strong> debuted an <a href="https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/acrab-unveils-glix-1-soc-and-agent-box-bringing-state-of-the-art-ai-to-the-edge-302833081.html">SoC for edge AI</a> that integrates CPU, GPU, and NPU resources with a unified memory architecture for large models.</li>
<li><strong>CAST</strong> updated its <a href="https://www.cast-inc.com/press-releases/cast-enhances-serial-memory-controller-ip-encryption-low-power-and-asil-ready">xSPI</a> serial memory controller IP core with AES encryption, AMBA power-state management, and programmable delay tuning.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Deployments</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Speedata</strong> deployed <strong>Arteris</strong>&#8216; FlexNoC technology in its processor for large-scale <a href="https://www.arteris.com/press-releases/arteris-deployed-by-speedata-for-data-center-compute/">data analytics</a> workloads.</li>
<li><strong>Ambiq</strong> expanded deployment of <strong>ChipAgents</strong>&#8216; <a href="https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260722612365/en/Ambiq-and-ChipAgents-Collaborate-to-Advance-Agentic-AI-for-Semiconductor-Engineering">agentic AI platform</a> for designing and verifying its ultra-low power edge AI chips.</li>
<li><strong>The Exploration Co.</strong> adopted <strong>Siemens</strong>&#8216; industrial software to develop <a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-the-exploration-company/">reusable spacecraft</a>.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<h2 id="Research"><strong>Research</strong></h2>
<p><strong>Cornell</strong> researchers showed that single-crystal niobium arsenide nanowires become more conductive as they shrink, offering a proof-of-concept <a href="https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2026/07/too-thin-fail-alternative-copper-microchip-interconnects">alternative to copper interconnects</a> at advanced nodes.</p>
<p class="isSelectedEnd"><strong>KAUST, MIT </strong>and other researchers showed that &#8220;a commercial 65nm CMOS process can be repurposed as a passive, <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18059">foundry-manufacturable characterization platform</a> by functionally partitioning its metal stack into microwave, thermal, and electrical subsystems within a 1 mm<sup>2</sup> footprint.&#8221;</p>
<p class="isSelectedEnd">A <strong>UCSD</strong> team developed an in-storage retrieval accelerator that embeds vector-search functions <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17538">directly into 3D NAND</a> to lower latency and energy for retrieval-augmented AI workloads.</p>
<p class="isSelectedEnd"><strong>Princeton</strong> researchers proposed <a href="https://semiengineering.com/hw-based-methods-to-dynamically-throttle-ai-performance-princeton-university/">HW mechanisms for dynamically throttling AI performance</a>, using microarchitecture-level controls such as cache way masking, bandwidth limits and latency insertion to constrain workloads at runtime.</p>
<h3><strong>More technical papers</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20141">Known Good Reliable Die Screening</a> in Chiplet-Based AI SoC (<strong>Qualcomm</strong>)</li>
<li><a href="https://pubs.aip.org/avs/jvb/article-abstract/44/4/043204/3397454/Through-silicon-via-etch-uniformity-enhancement?redirectedFrom=fulltext">TSV etch uniformity enhancement</a> and aspect-ratio influence on etch rate and profile (<strong>Hanyang, imec)</strong></li>
<li>Optimization of <a href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11614411">3D-DRAM Architecture</a> with Oxide-Semiconductor Channel through Process and Device Simulation (<strong>imec</strong> et al.)</li>
</ul>
<p>Find more industry research <a href="https://semiengineering.com/technical/">here</a>.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Security"><strong>Security</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Government guidance</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>ENISA</strong> published new <a href="https://www.enisa.europa.eu/publications/procurement-guidelines-for-the-cybersecurity-of-hospitals-and-healthcare-providers">healthcare cybersecurity procurement guidelines</a> urging buyers to require HW security features, signed firmware updates, device certificates, vulnerability-disclosure commitments, and timely patching for medical devices and connected systems.</li>
<li>The UK’s <strong>National Cyber Security Centre</strong> urged organizations to inventory systems that rely on cryptography and <a href="https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blogs/post-quantum-cryptography-pqc-migration-workshop-report">prepare for post-quantum migration</a>, targeting completed <a href="https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/pqc-migration-timelines">plans</a> by 2028, priority-system upgrades by 2031, and full migration by 2035.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Hacks and vulnerabilities</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>A hack of AI-music generation company <strong>Suno </strong>reportedly <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/21/ai-music-generator-suno-breach-affects-55m-users-per-have-i-been-pwned/">exposed 55 million</a> customers’ private information and revealed that the AI tool had scraped music from sites like <strong>YouTube, Genius </strong>and <strong>Deezer </strong>amid several ongoing copyright lawsuits against the company.</li>
<li>A cyberattack temporarily suspended U.S. production at Coca-Cola-owned fairlife. The <a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/gang-claims-responsibility-hack-coca-colas-fairlife-unit-2026-07-21/">Anubis group later claimed responsibility</a> and said it stole 1TB of data; Coca-Cola did not confirm that claim.</li>
<li><strong>Hikvision</strong> disclosed <a href="https://www.hikvision.com/europe/support/cybersecurity/security-advisory/security-vulnerabilities-in-some-hikvision-cameras/?">5 firmware vulnerabilities</a> affecting several IP-camera families.</li>
<li><strong>CISA</strong> posted new <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories">vulnerability alerts</a> this week.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>New security releases </strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Google</strong> released <a href="https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-3-6-flash-3-5-flash-lite-3-5-flash-cyber/">three new Gemini AI models,</a> including the security-focused Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber.</li>
<li>Researchers at <strong>DigiCert</strong> report <a href="https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/07/23/3332180/0/en/DigiCert-Research-Shows-Quantum-Security-Deployment-Remains-Stuck-Despite-Enterprise-Planning.html">that little progress has been made toward PQC security deployment</a>, despite widespread testing and fast-approaching regulatory deadlines. While 87% of organizations report they are planning, testing, or implementing PQC initiatives, only 7% of organizations have deployed quantum-safe or hybrid cryptography across most of their digital certificates, according to the researchers.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Security research papers</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16161">Fault Injection Planning</a> for Multi-Layer Self-Healing AI Infra. (<strong>Meta</strong> et al.)</li>
<li>Simulator for <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15782">Pre-silicon Power Side-Channel</a> Analysis (<strong>Radboud</strong>)</li>
<li><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19430">Safe Models Do Not Compose</a> into Safe Multi-Agent Systems (<strong>UCF</strong>)</li>
<li><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06963">LLMs and Gen AI</a> in Cybersecurity and Privacy (<strong>Virelya, Google</strong>)</li>
<li>Complete <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13939">PQC RISC-V eXtension Architecture</a> ( <strong>Politecnico di Torino</strong> et al.)</li>
<li><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18340">Quantum Cryptanalysis</a> on <strong>IBM</strong> Quantum HW (<strong>VIDRAFT</strong>)</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<h2><strong>Vehicles, Batteries</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Vehicle vulnerabilities</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>Researchers at <strong>UCSD</strong> found that more than 2 million cars with anti-theft systems installed by dealers had been put at risk by a <a href="https://today.ucsd.edu/story/2-million-cars-with-anti-theft-systems-installed-by-dealers-are-at-higher-risk-of-theft">Bluetooth vulnerability that allowed thieves to unlock car doors</a> using a smartphone app. The system developer released a patch for the issue this week.</li>
<li>AV-maker <strong>Zoox</strong> issued a software recall after one of its cars drove into an area clouded by heavy smoke from a <a href="https://www.fox5vegas.com/2026/07/20/zoox-issues-software-recall-after-robotaxi-drives-into-heavy-smoke-las-vegas/">nearby fire in Las Vegas</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Auto chips</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>NXP </strong><a href="https://www.nxp.com/company/about-nxp/newsroom/NW-NXP-INFOTAINMENT-CHIP-AI-ML-AUDIO">debuted the SAF9800</a>, a new automotive audio and radio processor designed to simplify infotainment architectures. The company said the processor was built through integrating analog radio and AI/ML-enabled audio processing into a single-chip solution.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Autonomous, connectivity, sensors</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>US legislators advanced the <a href="https://www.slotkin.senate.gov/2026/07/22/slotkin-moreno-bill-to-protect-national-economic-security-from-chinese-vehicles-advances-unanimously/">Connected Vehicle Security Act of 2026</a>, which would expand restrictions on Chinese-origin connected vehicles, SW, and HW beyond the existing BIS rule, adding new pressure on carmakers to scrub foreign-adversary technology from connected-car supply chains.</li>
<li><strong>Waymo</strong> L4 driverless vehicles in SF, Phoenix, LA, and Austin had <a href="https://www.iihs.org/research-areas/bibliography/ref/2374">68% fewer police-reportable crashes per mile</a> and a 91% lower rate of rear-ending another vehicle when compared to human drivers, reports <strong>IIHS</strong>.</li>
<li><strong>Tesla </strong>says it has logged <a href="https://assets-ir.tesla.com/tesla-contents/IR/TSLA-Q2-2026-Update.pdf">2.5M paid robotaxi miles</a> and will now offer service in <a href="https://twitter.com/robotaxi/status/2079551968725303500">Tampa and Orlando, Florida</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Mobileye&#8217;s</strong> advanced driving assistance and AV tech will be <a href="https://www.mobileye.com/news/mobileye-to-supply-cloud-enhanced-adas-for-select-future-stellantis-vehicles/">integrated in some Stellantis</a> vehicles starting in 2027. Also the company&#8217;s CEO <a href="https://www.mobileye.com/news/mobileye-announces-planned-leadership-transition/">stepped down</a>.</li>
<li><strong>SMP </strong>and <strong>Techstrong</strong> are jointly forming a new <a href="https://www.smpcorp.com/media/xw5nmhkn/smp-forms-joint-venture-with-techstrong-70626.pdf">Thai-based automotive sensor</a> company.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>EVs, batteries</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Ford</strong> will <a href="https://www.fromtheroad.ford.com/us/en/articles/2026/apple-maps-to-power-navigation-for-ford-universal-electric-vehicle">embed Apple Maps into its Universal EV Platform</a>, including EV routing and battery preconditioning.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-02150-y">Sodium-ion batteries</a> are nearing mass production as a cheaper, safer option for grid storage and lower-cost EVs, although their lower energy density limits wider use.</li>
<li><strong>Sila</strong> raised $300M to speed up its silicon-carbon (Si/C) anode <a href="https://www.silanano.com/press/press-releases/sila-secures-300-million-in-private-funding-to-ramp-gigascale-anode-manufacturing-and-strengthen-americas-technology-sovereignty">battery technology</a>.</li>
<li><strong>BC Hydro </strong>and the British Columbia government entered into a new partnership to triple the province’s <a href="https://news.gov.bc.ca/releases/2026ECS0041-000855">EV charging infrastructure</a> by 2035.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="Vehicles, Batteries"><strong>Vehicle research</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>UCLA, </strong><strong>U. of Rochester</strong>, and others demonstrated <a href="https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/biomedical-imaging-autonomous-vehicle-sensors-get-AI-boost">a physics-based ML imaging system</a> designed to capture details within “complex media.”  The system more than doubled the signal-to-noise ratio compared to a previous generation of the technology, with researchers suggesting that the system could power advances in AV sensor and biomedical imaging technology.</li>
<li><strong>NUS </strong>researchers developed an <a href="https://cde.nus.edu.sg/news/electronic-skin-that-senses-and-self-heals-under-water/">“electronic skin” for underwater diving devices</a> that are capable of detecting damage and autonomously self-healing while underwater.</li>
<li><strong>KAIST</strong> created an ultra-precise inspection technology to <a href="https://news.kaist.ac.kr/newsen/html/news/?mng_no=64830&amp;mode=V">prevent EV battery fires​</a>.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<h2 id="Trending Video"><strong>Trending Video</strong></h2>
<p><a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-models-on-the-edge/">AI Models On The Edge</a>: Moving from LLMs in the cloud to SLMs at the edge is much more complicated than just slimming down the algorithms. It requires changes in both HW and SW, and the constraints can vary greatly from one market segment to another. <strong>Quadric&#8217;s</strong> Daniel Firu and Ravi Chakaravarthy talk about how to optimize NPUs for different applications, how to build in enough flexibility to keep designs from becoming obsolete too quickly, and how to leverage the benefits of open-source while still adding value.</p>
<p><iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/LbgU5ybG4OY" width="480" height="270" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen="allowfullscreen"></iframe></p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Quantum"><strong>Quantum</strong></h2>
<p><strong>Hitachi </strong>is designing 100-qubit <a href="https://www.hitachi.com/content/dam/hitachi/global/en/press/files/2026/07/260722a.pdf">silicon quantum chips</a> that will be fabricated on Intel Foundry&#8217;s 18A process.</p>
<p><strong>Quantinuum</strong> and <strong>SoftBank</strong> published a roadmap to explore which quantum computing <a href="https://www.quantinuum.com/press-releases/quantinuum-and-softbank-corp-publish-joint-white-paper-on-scaling-practical-quantum-computing-use-cases-toward-the-fault-tolerant-era">use cases</a> will become feasible at what stage of hardware maturity.</p>
<p><strong>Photon Queue</strong> raised $4M to build <a href="https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260721058483/en/Photon-Queue-Raises-Oversubscribed-Seed-Round-to-Scale-Quantum-Memory-Systems">quantum memory</a> devices that store photons directly in free-space optical loops.</p>
<p><strong>PsiQuantum</strong> signed an expanded $125M deal with DARPA to continue work on the <a href="https://www.psiquantum.com/news-import/psiquantum-signs-125-million-agreement-with-darpa">Quantum Benchmarking Initiative</a>.</p>
<p><strong>Illinois </strong>received ~$30M in federal funding for <a href="https://gov-pritzker-newsroom.prezly.com/governor-pritzker-announces-30-million-eda-grant-for-advancing-quantum">quantum ecosystem</a> development.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Workforce, Education"><strong>Workforce, Education</strong></h2>
<p><strong>DHS’s</strong> final rule replaces open-ended “duration of status” for F, J and I nonimmigrants with <a href="https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/07/16/trump-administration-issues-final-rule-end-foreign-student-visa-abuse">fixed admission periods</a>. Also, USCIS says it <a href="https://www.uscis.gov/newsroom/alerts/uscis-reaches-fiscal-year-2027-h-1b-cap">received enough petitions</a> to meet both the 65,000 regular H-1B cap and the 20,000 advanced-degree exemption, or master’s cap, for FY 2027.</p>
<p>Security and ECE guru<strong> Mark Tehranipoor</strong> is now the <a href="https://news.ufl.edu/2026/07/engineering-dean/">dean of the University of Florida&#8217;s</a> College of Engineering.</p>
<p>The <strong>UK</strong> now has a <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/techfirst">semiconductor scholarship track</a> in its <strong>TechFirst</strong> program, offering students ~US$5K per year, industry connections and career support.</p>
<p><strong>ASML</strong> plans to offer eligible employees a conditional stock grant worth <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/world-at-work/asml-offer-employees-20000-retention-bonus-staying-2027-2030-2026-07-20/">€20,000 (about US$23K)</a> if they remain with the company from 2027 through 2030, Reuters reports.</p>
<p>An <strong>Economist tool</strong>: <a href="https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/2026/07/21/where-should-you-move-for-higher-pay">Where should you move for higher pay</a>?</p>
<hr />
